### I.—THE FIRST FUNERAL  
*(The first corpse I saw was on the German wires and could not be buried.)*

The whole field smelled so dreadful;  
We smelled the poor dog first.  
His horrid, swollen belly  
Looked ready to burst.  

His fur was most untidy;  
He hadn’t any eyes.  
It happened on Good Friday,  
And there were lots of flies.  

Then I felt the coldest  
I had ever felt—and sick;  
But Rose, because she’s the oldest,  
Dared poke him with her stick.  

He felt quite soft and horrid.  
The flies buzzed round his head  
And settled on his forehead.  
Rose whispered, “That dog’s dead.  

“You bury all dead people,  
When they are truly dead,  
Round churches with a steeple.  
Let’s bury this,” Rose said.  

“And let’s put mint all round him  
To hide the nasty smell.”  
I went to look and found it—  
Lots growing near the well.  

We poked him through the clover  
Into a hole, and then  
We threw brown earth right over  
And said, “Poor dog, amen.”
outputs.L2:
**I. – THE EARLIEST BURIAL**  
*(The first dead body I ever encountered lay tangled in the German wire, where no one could bury it.)*

A foul odor hung across the entire field. Before we saw the miserable dog, we noticed its smell. Its stomach was horribly bloated, as though it might explode, and its coat was disheveled. Its eyes were gone. This was on Good Friday, and flies were everywhere.

I suddenly felt colder than I had ever been and became nauseated. Rose, being the eldest, was brave enough to prod the animal with her stick. Its body was disgustingly soft. Flies hummed around its head and landed on its brow.

Rose quietly told me that the dog was dead. She said that once people are truly dead, they are buried beside steepled churches, so we ought to give the dog a burial too. She also suggested surrounding it with mint to cover the awful odor.

I searched for some and discovered plenty growing beside the well. Using sticks, we pushed the dog through the clover and into a hollow. Then we covered it completely with brown soil and finished by saying, “Poor dog. Amen.”

The speaker recalls an upsetting experience that took place on Good Friday, when the children discovered a dead dog lying in a foul-smelling field. The animal was badly decomposed: its body was swollen, its eyes were missing, and flies surrounded the corpse. The disturbing sight and terrible smell made the speaker feel cold and sick.

Rose, the oldest of the children, showed more courage than the others. She reached out and touched the dog, confirming that it was truly dead. Because the children believed that every dead creature deserved to be buried, they decided to hold a funeral for it. They gathered mint and placed it around the body to cover the unpleasant smell, then buried the dog beneath the earth. Finally, they marked its passing with the simple, compassionate words, “Poor dog, Amen!”
outputs.L4:
The poem portrays a group of children encountering death for the first time when they discover the decomposing body of a dog. The sight is disturbing and unfamiliar, forcing them to confront the physical reality of mortality. At first, the dog’s decay inspires horror and perhaps curiosity, but the children do not abandon or mistreat it. Instead, they respond by drawing on the religious customs they have observed in the adult world.

Imitating a Christian funeral, the children carefully bury the animal with mint and earth and offer a prayer. Their ceremony may be simple and imperfect, yet it is sincere. The mint introduces an image of freshness and sweetness that contrasts sharply with decomposition, while the earth both conceals the body and returns it to nature. Through these gestures, the children transform something frightening and repulsive into an occasion for tenderness and respect.

The burial shows how ritual helps people make sense of experiences that are otherwise difficult to understand. Although the children may not fully comprehend death or Christian teachings, they recognize that the dead deserve care and dignity. By repeating familiar customs, they create order in the face of mortality and express compassion for a creature that can no longer receive it. The poem therefore presents innocence not as ignorance, but as a source of moral sensitivity: confronted with death, the children instinctively answer horror with kindness.

# THE FIRST FUNERAL

Before death had a name, the people believed that every silence would eventually end.

They waited beside the old hunter for three days. They warmed his hands near the fire, offered him water, and called him by all the names he had carried—son, brother, husband, father. But he did not answer. His chest remained still, and his eyes seemed fixed on something beyond the sky.

On the fourth morning, a child asked, “Where has he gone?”

No one knew.

The oldest woman in the village knelt beside him. She washed the dust from his face and combed the leaves from his hair. Then she wrapped him in the hide of the first deer he had hunted as a boy.

“We cannot leave him here,” she said. “The rain will come. The animals will come. We must give him a place where he can rest.”

So the people dug beneath an ancient tree whose roots rose from the earth like the hands of giants. Into the grave, they placed the hunter’s spear, a bowl of berries, a flint for making fire, and a necklace his daughter had made from shells.

“Why give him these things?” someone asked.

“In case the road is long,” the old woman replied.

They lowered him into the ground as the sun sank. At first, no one moved. Covering him with earth felt cruel, like closing a door while someone was still inside.

Then the hunter’s daughter took a handful of soil.

“Goodbye,” she whispered, though the word had never before been used in that way.

One by one, the others did the same.

When the grave was filled, they stood around it and told stories. They spoke of the time the hunter had crossed a flooded river to save a stranger. They remembered how loudly he laughed and how badly he sang. Slowly, their sorrow changed. It did not disappear, but it became something they could carry together.

Before leaving, the child placed a small yellow flower on the fresh earth.

That night, the people returned to their homes knowing two things they had not known before: that a life could end, and that love could remain after it.

And so **THE FIRST FUNERAL** was not only the beginning of mourning.

It was the beginning of memory.
